questions.q: Why can an LLM state something false in a confident, fluent tone?
options: Its training objective rewards plausible next tokens, and nothing in it separates likely-sounding text from true text
It deliberately lies when it does not know the answer
It always retrieves facts from a live database that is sometimes out of date
Fluent text is only produced when the model is certain of the facts
questions.explain: Next-token prediction generates what fits the pattern. As the bigram demo showed, a fluent sentence can be one that was never in the training data.

questions.q: In the bigram demo, what did "the customer renewed the report ." illustrate?
options: A memorized sentence copied from the corpus
A locally fluent sentence that was never in the training text, like a hallucination
A bug caused by a bad random seed
The model correctly generalizing a true fact
questions.explain: Each word pair occurred in the corpus, but the full sentence did not: plausible, novel, and unsupported.

questions.q: You need an LLM-based tool to report an exact sum over 10,000 rows. What is the safest approach from this lesson?
options: Ask the model to add the numbers mentally and trust the result
Raise the temperature to improve accuracy
Have the model write code or call a tool, then run it to get the exact value
Shorten the prompt so the model concentrates
questions.explain: Exact arithmetic and multi-step calculation are unreliable in the model itself, so delegate them to code.

questions.q: A stand-in model scores 17 of 20 (85 percent) with a 95 percent Wilson interval of about 0.64 to 0.95. What should you conclude?
options: The true accuracy is exactly 85 percent
The true accuracy is certainly above 95 percent
The interval proves the model is broken
With only 20 examples the estimate is imprecise, so small gains like 85 to 90 percent are not reliable evidence
questions.explain: A wide interval from a small sample means differences of a few points are within noise. Use a larger labeled set.

questions.q: Which practice is recommended when using an LLM as a judge of open-ended answers?
options: Trust it fully because LLMs are unbiased
Calibrate it against human labels, since it has its own biases
Use the same examples in the judge prompt and in the evaluation set
Never evaluate open-ended text at all
questions.explain: LLM judges are useful but biased, so check how well they agree with human labels.
